newsitem.title: DENMARK: U.S. film director sues Danish television.
newsitem.headline: U.S. film director sues Danish television.

text.p: A Danish court Monday began hearing a lawsuit by Oscar-winning director Sydney Pollack against Danish government television for screening one of this films in a drastically reduced format.
Pollack, championed here by the Danish Film Directors' Association, is seeking 100,000 crowns ($16,100) for alleged damage to his professional reputation.
But more than money, they hope to win greater legal protection for artistic works.
"This is the first case against (the technique called) pan scanning in Denmark and, I believe, anywhere," association Chairman Knud Hauge said in an interview.

"I hope that if we win, it could influence copyright law in the United States, Britain and elsewhere," he said, adding that a 1991 French court ban on the colourization of John Huston's black and white film "Asphalt Jungle" was imitated by other countries.

The new case involves the television broadcast in 1991 of Pollack's Cinemascope film "Three Days of the Condor" in a pan scanned version, a technique which in adapting the film for the small screen cuts the visible picture by over 50 percent.
Pollack says the process erased material in the periphery of the picture, placed there to show lurking danger and create a mood of paranoia.
"The pan scan picks out only the main figures as the centre of interest and thus changes the intensity, pace and timing of a film," a statement by the association said.
Danish State Radio international programme Director Finn Rowold said that distributors, not broadcasters, determined the format of a film to be televised.

"We always try and get hold of films in their original format from distributors, but sometimes this is not possible," he said. "If the distributor cannot provide us with an original version of a film, we have to show a pan scanned copy."
Pollack, 62, won an Oscar in 1986 for "Out of Africa" -- starring Meryl Streep and Robert Redford -- based on the book by Danish baroness Karen Blixen.

The court case, in which Pollack is supported by the Danish directors, the European Directors' Guild and the Hollywood-based Artists' Rights Foundation is expected to close Tuesday, with a judgment possible next month.
Although the copyright in "Three Days of the Condor" is owned by its producers, Danish law gives permanent rights to artists, regardless of subsequent ownership of their work.
